title: Python Decorators: Write a Timer and a Cache
audience: Developers with a few months of Python experience who have seen the @ syntax but never written a decorator.
brief: Practical tutorial. The opening promises viewers will write a timing decorator and a caching decorator. Goal: viewers star the example repo linked in the description.

issues.description: The first 15 seconds are vague filler ('a thing in Python... a feature') that never says what decorators do or why the viewer should care.
Says decorators arrived in Python 3.9 in 2020. They were introduced in Python 2.4 in 2004 (PEP 318).
A roughly 40-second rant about tabs versus spaces, Neovim and a mechanical keyboard that is unrelated to decorators.
Spends over 30 seconds re-explaining what a function is, in repeated phrasing, to an audience that already writes Python.
The opening promises a caching decorator, but only the timing decorator is built; the video ends after asserting 'caching builds on the same idea'.

lines.text: So, um, today we are going to talk about a thing in Python.
It's a feature. It's one that people use.
I think it is a pretty interesting thing, so let's, you know, get into it, I guess.
By the end of this video, you will write two decorators: one that times any function, and one that caches its results.
Decorators have been part of Python since version three point nine, which came out in twenty twenty, and they have become really popular since.
Let's start with functions.
A function is a block of code that you can call by name.
You define it with the def keyword, you give it a name, and then you call it.
Remember, a function is just a block of code with a name, so when I call a function, I am running that block of code.
So again, you define a function, you name it, and you call it by its name to run the code inside.
A decorator is a function that takes another function and returns a new one.
Let's write a timing decorator. We import time, then define timer, which takes a function.
Inside it we define wrapper. Wrapper records the start time, calls the function, records the end time, and prints how long it took.
Then timer returns wrapper. Finally, we put at timer above any function, and that function is timed.
Now, I know some of you will ask what editor I am using, and honestly, this is where I need to rant about tabs versus spaces.
I think tabs are objectively better, because you can set your own width, and people who use spaces are, frankly, wrong.
My old team lead used spaces, and we argued about this for two years.
I use Neovim, by the way, with a custom config, and I have been meaning to make a video about that config.
I should also do one about my mechanical keyboard, which has these amazing brown switches.
Okay. Back to decorators.
So that's the timing decorator, and now you know how decorators work.
Caching builds on exactly the same idea.
If you want the code, star the example repo linked in the description.
Thanks for watching.
